q-6190.name: Question 1
q-6190.problem: Express $\frac{1}{81}$ as a base raised to a negative exponent.
q-6190.worked_solution:
First, we write $\frac{1}{81}$ as a base raised to a power:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{81} & =\frac{1\times 1}{9\times 9} \\  & =\frac{1}{9}\times \frac{1}{9} \\  & ={(\frac{1}{9})}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we find the reciprocal of the base $(\frac{1}{9}),$ and then raise that reciprocal to the same power but with the *opposite* sign $(-2),$ as follows:

$$
{(\frac{1}{9})}^{2}={9}^{-2}
$$

q-6194.name: Question 2
q-6194.problem: Express $\frac{1}{64}$ as a base raised to a negative exponent.
q-6194.worked_solution:
First, we write $\frac{1}{64}$ as a power with a negative exponent.

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{64} & =\frac{1\times 1\times 1}{4\times 4\times 4} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\times \frac{1}{4}\times \frac{1}{4} \\  & ={(\frac{1}{4})}^{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we find the reciprocal of the base $(\frac{1}{4}),$ and then raise that reciprocal to the same power but with the *opposite* sign $(-3),$ as follows:

$$
{(\frac{1}{4})}^{3}={4}^{-3}
$$

q-71764.name: Question 3
q-71764.worked_solution:
We find the reciprocal of the base $(\frac{3}{4})$, and then raise that reciprocal to the same power but with the *opposite* sign $(+2)$, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{(\frac{3}{4})}^{-2} & ={(\frac{4}{3})}^{2} \\  & =\frac{4}{3}\cdot \frac{4}{3} \\  & =\frac{16}{9}\end{aligned}
$$
